app.notes: Flight Path is a client-only Three.js/Vite app with no backend, accounts, API keys or external services. The only outside reference is a plain GitHub link in the UI; the Earth texture (world.topo.jpg) and plane SVGs are bundled locally. Built with Node 22.12.0, pinned in mise.toml, using `npm ci` and `npx vite build --base=/ --outDir .ui-capture/out` (see .ui-capture/build.sh). The --base=/ flag overrides the repo's GitHub Pages base of '/flight-path/' so the build works from the root of a static server. No source files were changed. Data: the app ships its own real-world dataset in src/common/Data.ts, 34,298 departure/arrival airport coordinate pairs compiled into the bundle. By default it renders 5,000 of them as animated, GPU-instanced planes on dashed great-circle arcs, colored by region. The app keeps no state (no localStorage or URL params), so there is no user data to seed. Main areas: a full-screen 3D globe with a photorealistic Earth texture, atmosphere, day/night shading driven by the real UTC sun position, a starfield and orbit camera controls; an FPS stats panel; and a dat.GUI control panel, collapsed by default per a recent commit, with folders for Flight Controls (flight count 1-30,000, return flights), Flight Path (dash length/gap, hide path), Plane Controls (size, color, speed, elevation, SVG/shape style, hide), Earth Controls (day/night, atmosphere, real-time sun, UTC time slider) and Brightness. A WebGL-capable browser is required. The 18 MB texture loads before the scene appears.

- Follow the repo's own setup docs and tooling. Take the simplest route that shows the real app: a static production build if the front end works without a backend, otherwise the app's own server (production or dev mode).

# Tools: use mise
Install every runtime and tool you need (node, the package manager, python, bun, ...) with mise, pinned to exact versions in a mise.toml at the repo root, so the setup can be reproduced. Match what the repo asks for (engines, .nvmrc, .tool-versions, packageManager). mise is already configured for this directory: `mise install` installs into ./.ui-capture/mise, and its shims come first on PATH, so `node`, `pnpm` and the rest resolve to the pinned versions. Don't use other copies of these tools or download runtimes by hand.

# Secrets, API keys and external services: fake them
The app must not depend on anything outside this machine, and when it runs it has no network except localhost. Wherever it expects secrets, environment variables, API keys or third-party services (hosted auth or OAuth, payment providers, email, LLM or other AI APIs, maps, storage buckets, analytics, hosted databases):
- Give the required variables placeholder values so the app starts.
- Where it actually calls the service, make the call succeed locally with realistic responses: use the app's own mock, test or offline mode if it has one; otherwise point the client at a small local stub server that start.sh also starts, or swap in a stub at the integration boundary (the API client or service module). Keep stubs out of UI code. Responses should look like what the real service returns for a real user, e.g. an AI reply that actually answers, a payment history with real-looking amounts.
- Calls the browser makes directly to outside services count too; point them at the local stub.
- For sign-in through an outside provider, create a local account or use the app's dev sign-in so you can get past it.

Seed it the way an established user's data would look after months of actual use: specific, plausible names and content for this kind of app; dates spread over time; a realistic mix of states (done, in progress, overdue, archived, ...); realistic volume (dozens to hundreds of records where the app revolves around records); short and long text; some messiness real data has. Start from the app's own demo or seed data if it has realistic data, and extend it if it's thin. Load data through the app's own paths (its API, import, seed scripts, or its database schema), never by hardcoding it into UI code. If the app needs an account, create one and attach the data to it. A process you start in the background can't be seen or stopped from a later command, so test servers on another port than 4463 (e.g. 5463) or in the foreground under `timeout`; anything still listening on 4463 is stopped before I check.

- app.json: {"mode": "static" or "server", "entry": "/path where the main UI opens", "login": null or {"username": "...", "email": "...", "password": "..."}, "stubs": [{"service": "what was faked", "how": "how"}], "notes": "how you set it up, what data is loaded, and the main areas of the app"}
- static mode: the production build in ./.ui-capture/out, with index.html as its entry. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server; unknown paths fall back to index.html.

It runs with the same PATH and restrictions as your shell, plus no network at all except localhost, so everything must already be installed, built and seeded (or seeded by start.sh itself).
